facts.fact: Economic growth is a narrow, quantitative concept — a rise in real output or income that can be measured in absolute terms.
Economists define economic growth as the process whereby the real per capita income of a country increases over a long period.
Economic development is multidimensional: growth plus reduction of poverty, inequality and unemployment and qualitative change.
Growth is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for development.
Under the traditional approach, economic development means a sustained increase in real per capita income, and growth and development are used as synonyms.
Under the new approach, development is a rise in real per capita income over a long period along with reduction of poverty, inequality and unemployment.
A rise in absolute and per-capita real GNP does not connote higher development if poverty and unemployment increase.
Development, unlike growth, includes changes in the composition of output and the allocation of resources to sectors such as agriculture and industry.
Development involves changes in social structure, attitudes and institutions, which makes it harder to realise than growth.
'Jobless growth' describes years in which GDP grew rapidly while employment generation lagged, especially in the organised sector.
Inclusive growth is growth whose benefits spread across regions, sectors and social groups, reducing poverty and inequality.
Economic growth occurs through capital formation (UPSC 2013).
Despite high savings, capital formation may not raise output much if the capital-output ratio (ICOR) is high.
ICOR (Incremental Capital-Output Ratio) = additional investment ÷ additional output; a high ICOR signals inefficient use of capital.
Human capital formation raises the knowledge, skill levels and capacities of people and adds to intangible wealth (UPSC 2018).
The source lists four development indices: HDI, IHDI (Inequality-adjusted HDI), GDI (Gender Development Index) and AHDI (Augmented HDI).
The three-sector classification of the economy is associated with A.G.B. Fisher and Colin Clark (Fisher-Clark hypothesis).
W. Arthur Lewis (1954) gave the dual-sector model in which surplus labour moves from the traditional to the modern sector.
W.W. Rostow's stages of growth include traditional society, pre-conditions, take-off, drive to maturity and high mass consumption.
Amartya Sen's capability approach sees development as the expansion of the real freedoms people enjoy ('Development as Freedom').
GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA).
GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced within the domestic territory of a country in a year.
GNP is the value of final goods and services produced by the nationals of a country, whether living within the country or outside.
Per capita income = National income ÷ Population.
If NFIA is negative, GNP is smaller than GDP.
Only final goods and services are counted in GDP so that intermediate goods are not double counted.
GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100.
Factor cost = Market price − indirect taxes + subsidies.
The expenditure method adds C + I + G + (X − M).
The primary sector covers activities that directly use natural resources — agriculture, fishing, forestry, dairy farming and mining.
Dairy farming is a primary-sector activity (UPSC 2024).
Mining / mineral exploration is a primary-sector activity, not tertiary (UPSC 2024).
Weaving cloth (cotton into yarn and cloth) is a secondary-sector activity (UPSC 2024).
Storage of agricultural produce (warehouses, godowns) is a tertiary-sector activity, not secondary (UPSC 2024).
Converting sugarcane into sugar or gur in a mill is a secondary-sector activity.
Construction (making bricks from earth and clay) is part of the secondary sector.
The secondary (industrial) sector transforms raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods; it rose to prominence with the Industrial Revolution.
The tertiary (service) sector supports production and produces no tangible goods.
Modern tertiary activities include internet cafes, ATM booths, call centres and software companies.
The quaternary sector covers knowledge-based activities — R&D, IT, education, consulting.
The quinary sector covers top-level decision-making and policy roles (gold-collar).
In developed countries the dominant sector shifted from primary to secondary (Industrial Revolution) and then to tertiary.
The tertiary sector has grown fastest in India because of the IT boom, urbanisation and higher demand for services.
The services (tertiary) sector contributes the largest share of India's GVA (~55%).
Approximate current GVA shares: services ~54.7%, industry ~27.6%, agriculture ~17.7%.
Agriculture has the highest workforce share but the lowest GVA per worker.
Agriculture employs about 46% of India's workers (PLFS 2023-24).
India moved from agriculture to services, largely skipping a strong manufacturing-led phase.
The fall in agriculture's GVA share has not been matched by an equal fall in its workforce share.
At independence about 70–75% of India's workforce depended on agriculture.
Real-sector activities produce goods and services (a farmer harvesting, a textile mill making fabric); bank lending and bond issues are financial-sector activities (UPSC 2022).
Fixed capital is durable and used repeatedly — a computer, machinery or a farmer's plough (UPSC 2024).
Working capital is used up in one use — petrol, raw materials, yarn used by a weaver (UPSC 2024).
The organised sector is government-regulated and gives job security, fixed hours, pensions and other benefits.
The unorganised sector is unregulated, casual and lacks social security, yet dominates employment.
Daily wage labourers, street vendors and small unregistered shops are examples of the unorganised sector.
Informal employment accounts for about 87% of India's workers (ILO, 2025).
The public sector aims at public welfare and essential services; the private sector aims at profit.
Indian Railways, public sector banks and Bharat Petroleum are public-sector examples; Reliance, Tata and Infosys are private-sector examples.
A sunrise industry is a sector in its infancy with high growth potential — e.g. IT, healthcare, telecom, retail.
Pink-collar jobs are caregiving service roles traditionally associated with women, such as nursing and daycare.
White-collar jobs are professional and office roles such as accountants, lawyers and IT professionals.
Blue-collar jobs are manual labour and skilled trades such as electricians, plumbers and factory workers.
Green-collar jobs are environment and sustainability jobs such as solar technicians.
Grey-collar jobs combine technical and physical skill — paramedics, firefighters, technicians.
Gold-collar jobs are highly skilled professionals such as doctors, scientists and CEOs.
Red-collar jobs are public-sector and emergency services such as police and government workers.
Black-collar jobs are hazardous or informal roles such as miners, sanitation workers and oil drillers.
The eight core industries are coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilizers, steel, cement and electricity.
Textiles (and automobiles) are not among the eight core industries (UPSC 2012).
The eight core industries together carry about 40.27% of the weight of items in the IIP.
Refinery products have the highest weight (28.04%) in the Index of Eight Core Industries (base 2011-12).
Electricity (19.85%) is second and steel (17.92%) third in the core-industries weights.
Fertilizers have the lowest weight (2.63%) among the eight core industries.
Coal 10.33%, crude oil 8.98%, natural gas 6.88% and cement 5.37% are the remaining core-industry weights.
The Index of Eight Core Industries is released monthly by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT (Ministry of Commerce and Industry).
In the older 2004-05 series electricity had the highest core-industry weight, which is why the UPSC 2015 key says electricity.
The core-industries index tracks the monthly performance of key sectors and serves as an indicator of industrial performance.
India is a lower-middle-income economy in the World Bank classification.
India's nominal per-capita GDP is about US$2,750 (IMF, 2026).
Economic dualism means a modern sector coexists with a traditional subsistence sector.
A mixed economy is one in which public and private sectors coexist with state planning.
India adopted the mixed-economy model through the Industrial Policy Resolutions of 1948 and 1956.
India's mixed economy has been progressively liberalised since 1991.
Capital deficiency (low per-capita capital, low capital formation) is a feature of India as a developing economy.
Heavy dependence of the workforce on agriculture is a feature of the Indian economy.
Disguised unemployment means more workers are engaged than needed; removing them does not reduce output.
Over-population and a high dependency burden are features of the Indian economy, though the age structure now favours a demographic dividend.
The demographic dividend is the growth potential from a rising share of the working-age (15–59) population.
India is the 3rd largest economy by PPP but ranks lower by nominal GDP.
India's nominal GDP is about US$4.06 trillion, 6th largest in the IMF April 2026 WEO.
India became the 4th largest economy by nominal GDP in 2025, overtaking Japan (NITI Aayog).
Achievements since 1947 include Green Revolution food self-sufficiency, a world-class IT/services industry and a diversified industrial base.
India's consumption Gini index is about 25.5 (World Bank).
HDI combines health (life expectancy), education (schooling) and standard of living (GNI per capita).
HDI was introduced by UNDP in 1990, conceived by Mahbub-ul-Haq with Amartya Sen.
India's HDI is 0.685, rank 130 of 193, in the Medium category (HDR 2025).
The 17 SDGs were adopted by all UN member states in 2015 to be achieved by 2030.
Black money is income on which due tax is unpaid, or wealth concealed from the authorities (the parallel economy).
The main worry about black money for the Government is loss of revenue to the State Exchequer due to tax evasion (UPSC 2011/2021).
The SIT on Black Money (2014) was headed by Justice M.B. Shah on a Supreme Court direction.
Justice Arijit Pasayat was the Vice-Chairman of the SIT on Black Money.
PMLA 2002 came into force in 2005 and is India's principal anti-money-laundering law.
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) investigates offences under the PMLA.
Money laundering proceeds through placement, layering and integration.
FIU-IND receives suspicious transaction reports.
The Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015 targets undisclosed foreign income and assets.
The Benami Transactions Amendment Act 2016 and the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018 are separate laws from the 2015 Black Money Act.
BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting) is an OECD initiative to curb tax avoidance by multinational companies (UPSC 2016).
Andhra Pradesh's GSDP (current prices) is projected at about ₹19.75 lakh crore for 2026-27.
AP's per-capita GSDP (2024-25) of about ₹2.98 lakh is above the national average (~₹2.35 lakh).
AP's primary sector contributes about 37% of GSVA (2024-25), about double the all-India share (~18%).
AP's industry and services shares of GSVA (2024-25) are about 21% and 42%.
Andhra Pradesh's GSDP grew about 8% (constant prices) in 2024-25, faster than India's 6.5%.
Andhra Pradesh is the largest producer of fish and aquaculture (shrimp) in India.
AP's primary sector share is notably larger than the all-India average — AP is agrarian-heavy.
